2.1.6-software-generation-cs1004.json.title: Generate and sanity-check Poisson and Exponential draws
2.1.6-software-generation-cs1004.json.problem_statement: An analyst needs software samples from two univariate families before any joint modelling: (i) annual claim counts as Poisson(λ = 3); (ii) inter-claim waiting times (days) as Exponential with mean θ = 5. Describe the generation plan for n = 50 draws of each family, state one sanity check for each sample, and decide whether a mean of 3.1 on the Poisson sample alone proves the software call was correct.

given.note: illustrative software output for the refuse step

2.1.6-software-generation-cs1004.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Name a sampler for each family, one check against support or mean, then judge whether 3.1 alone certifies the Poisson call.

steps.label: Plan the two software samplers
steps.attempt_cue: Name a discrete call for Poisson(3) and a continuous call for Exponential mean 5.
steps.explanation: Software generation starts from a named family and parameter, not from a blank RNG. Poisson uses a discrete count sampler; Exponential uses a positive continuous sampler with mean 5 (or rate 1/5, depending on the package convention).
steps.calculation: Poisson: rpois / Poisson(3); Exponential: rexp(mean=5) or Exp(rate=0.2)
steps.result: Two named samplers, parameters fixed before drawing

steps.label: Run one sanity check per sample
steps.attempt_cue: State a support check and a rough mean check.
steps.explanation: A usable check compares sample behaviour with the family's support and first moment. Poisson draws must be non-negative integers with sample mean near 3; Exponential draws must be strictly positive with sample mean near 5.
steps.calculation: Poisson: all ≥ 0 integers, mean ≈ 3; Exponential: all > 0, mean ≈ 5
steps.result: Support + rough mean check for each family

steps.label: Refuse mean-near-target as sole proof
steps.attempt_cue: Decide whether sample mean 3.1 alone proves the Poisson call was correct.
steps.explanation: A sample mean near λ is consistent with Poisson(3) but does not by itself prove the call, the seed, or the parameterisation. Generation without a support/parameter check, and without refusing overclaim that univariate sampling finishes joint work, is incomplete.
steps.calculation: 3.1 ≈ 3 is consistent, not a proof of correct generation
steps.result: Mean proximity alone does not certify the sampler

2.1.6-software-generation-cs1004.json.final_answer: Generate n = 50 from Poisson(3) and Exponential(mean 5) with named software samplers; check support and rough means; a Poisson sample mean of 3.1 is consistent but not sole proof that the call was correct.
2.1.6-software-generation-cs1004.json.common_pitfall: Treating any code that prints numbers as generation complete, or treating a sample mean near 3 as proof the Poisson(3) call was correct without checking support, parameterisation, or that joint distributions remain out of scope.

2.2.1-marginal-conditional-cs1005.json.title: Marginal and conditional from a flood-wind property table
2.2.1-marginal-conditional-cs1005.json.problem_statement: A property book records indicators (X, Y) with joint PMF P(0,0) = 0.55, P(0,1) = 0.15, P(1,0) = 0.20, P(1,1) = 0.10, where X = 1 if a flood claim occurs and Y = 1 if a wind claim occurs in the same year. Compute P(Y = 1) and P(X = 1 | Y = 1).
2.2.1-marginal-conditional-cs1005.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Sum the Y = 1 column for the marginal, then divide the joint cell by that marginal for the conditional.

steps.label: Form the marginal P(Y = 1)
steps.attempt_cue: Add the joint probabilities with Y = 1.
steps.explanation: The marginal for Y = 1 sums over X: P(Y = 1) = P(0,1) + P(1,1).

steps.label: Form the conditional P(X = 1 | Y = 1)
steps.attempt_cue: Divide P(1,1) by P(Y = 1).
steps.explanation: Conditional probability renormalises the joint cell by the matching marginal.

steps.label: Refuse joint-as-marginal
steps.attempt_cue: State why P(1,1) = 0.10 is not P(Y = 1).
steps.explanation: A single joint cell is not a marginal. Marginals sum across the other variable; conditionals divide by that sum.

2.2.1-marginal-conditional-cs1005.json.final_answer: P(Y = 1) = 0.25; P(X = 1 | Y = 1) = 0.40. The joint table is not interchangeable with its margins or conditionals without these moves.
2.2.1-marginal-conditional-cs1005.json.common_pitfall: Reporting P(Y = 1) = 0.10 because that is the flood-and-wind cell, or taking P(X = 1 | Y = 1) = 0.10 without dividing by the marginal 0.25.

2.2.3-cov-corr-expectation-cs1005.json.title: Covariance, correlation, and E[X+2Y] from a joint PMF
2.2.3-cov-corr-expectation-cs1005.json.problem_statement: Two binary indicators (X, Y) for a household have joint PMF P(0,0) = 0.30, P(0,1) = 0.20, P(1,0) = 0.20, P(1,1) = 0.30, where X = 1 if a contents claim occurs and Y = 1 if a buildings claim occurs. Compute Cov(X, Y), Corr(X, Y), and E[X + 2Y].
2.2.3-cov-corr-expectation-cs1005.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Form E[X], E[Y], and E[XY] first, then Cov, then Corr, then E[X+2Y] by linearity.

steps.label: Compute the first moments
steps.attempt_cue: Find E[X], E[Y], and E[XY] from the joint table.
steps.explanation: For binary indicators, E[X] = P(X = 1) and E[Y] = P(Y = 1). The product moment is E[XY] = P(X = 1, Y = 1).

steps.label: Form Cov and Corr
steps.attempt_cue: Use Cov = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y] and divide by σ_X σ_Y.
steps.explanation: Covariance subtracts the product of means from E[XY]. Each margin is Bernoulli(0.5), so Var(X) = Var(Y) = 0.25 and σ_X = σ_Y = 0.5.

steps.label: Evaluate E[X + 2Y] and refuse Corr=0⇒independence
steps.attempt_cue: Apply linearity, then state why Corr ≠ 0 here does not finish an independence claim.
steps.explanation: Linearity gives E[X + 2Y] = E[X] + 2E[Y] without needing the joint again. Correlation here is 0.20, not zero; even Corr = 0 would not by itself prove independence for general joint distributions.
steps.result: E[X + 2Y] = 1.50; Corr ≠ 0 here (and Corr = 0 ≠ independence in general)

2.2.3-cov-corr-expectation-cs1005.json.final_answer: Cov(X, Y) = 0.05; Corr(X, Y) = 0.20; E[X + 2Y] = 1.50. Zero correlation is not automatic independence, and here correlation is not zero.
2.2.3-cov-corr-expectation-cs1005.json.common_pitfall: Computing Cov as E[XY] alone (forgetting to subtract E[X]E[Y]), or claiming that Corr = 0 would prove independence for any joint distribution.

2.2.4-linear-combinations-cs1005.json.title: Mean and variance of 2X − Y with nonzero covariance
2.2.4-linear-combinations-cs1005.json.problem_statement: Portfolio losses X and Y (£000) satisfy E[X] = 10, E[Y] = 4, Var(X) = 9, Var(Y) = 4, and Cov(X, Y) = 3. For the linear combination L = 2X − Y, compute E[L] and Var(L).
2.2.4-linear-combinations-cs1005.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Apply linearity for the mean, then expand Var(2X − Y) including the covariance term.

steps.label: Compute E[2X − Y]
steps.attempt_cue: Use E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y] with a = 2, b = −1.
steps.explanation: Expectation is linear whether or not X and Y are dependent.

steps.label: Expand Var(2X − Y)
steps.attempt_cue: Write a²Var(X) + b²Var(Y) + 2ab Cov(X, Y).
steps.explanation: Variance of a linear combination needs the covariance whenever dependence is present. Here a = 2 and b = −1, so 2ab Cov = 2(2)(−1)(3) = −12.

steps.label: Refuse dropping Cov
steps.attempt_cue: State the incorrect variance obtained if Cov is ignored.
steps.explanation: Dropping the covariance term as if X and Y were uncorrelated gives 36 + 4 = 40, which overstates Var(L) when Cov = 3 > 0 and the combination is 2X − Y.

2.2.4-linear-combinations-cs1005.json.final_answer: E[2X − Y] = 16; Var(2X − Y) = 28. Omitting Cov(X, Y) = 3 incorrectly yields 40.
2.2.4-linear-combinations-cs1005.json.common_pitfall: Computing Var(2X − Y) as 4Var(X) + Var(Y) = 40 and dropping the covariance term even though Cov(X, Y) = 3 is given.

2.3.1-conditional-expectation-cs1006.jso.title: Conditional mean severity given claim count
2.3.1-conditional-expectation-cs1006.jso.problem_statement: Claim count X and severity band Y (£00) have joint PMF P(1,10) = 0.25, P(1,20) = 0.25, P(2,10) = 0.15, P(2,20) = 0.35. Compute E[Y | X = 1] and E[Y | X = 2], and state why neither equals the unconditional E[Y] as an object.
2.3.1-conditional-expectation-cs1006.jso.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Form P(X = x), then weight the Y values by the conditional probabilities given X = x.

steps.label: Form the X margins
steps.attempt_cue: Sum the joint cells for X = 1 and for X = 2.
steps.explanation: Conditional expectation renormalises the joint slice for fixed X by the marginal P(X = x).

steps.label: Evaluate E[Y | X = 1] and E[Y | X = 2]
steps.attempt_cue: Compute the conditional means from the renormalised joints.
steps.explanation: E[Y | X = x] = Σ y P(X = x, Y = y) / P(X = x).

steps.label: Refuse equating E[Y] with E[Y|X]
steps.attempt_cue: Compute E[Y] and contrast it with the conditional means as objects.
steps.explanation: The unconditional mean E[Y] = 10×0.40 + 20×0.60 = 16 is a single number. E[Y|X] is a random function of X (15 when X = 1, 17 when X = 2). They are related by the tower law but are not the same object.

2.3.1-conditional-expectation-cs1006.jso.final_answer: E[Y | X = 1] = 15; E[Y | X = 2] = 17. Unconditional E[Y] = 16 is a number; E[Y|X] is a function of X.
2.3.1-conditional-expectation-cs1006.jso.common_pitfall: Reporting E[Y | X = 1] = 10×0.25 + 20×0.25 = 7.5 without dividing by P(X = 1), or treating the unconditional mean 16 as interchangeable with E[Y|X].

2.3.2-mean-variance-conditioning-cs1006..title: Tower law and variance decomposition for claim cost
2.3.2-mean-variance-conditioning-cs1006..problem_statement: A risk type indicator X equals 0 with probability 0.4 and 1 with probability 0.6. Conditional on X, claim cost Y (£00) satisfies E[Y | X = 0] = 5, E[Y | X = 1] = 12, Var(Y | X = 0) = 4, and Var(Y | X = 1) = 9. Compute E[Y] and Var(Y) using the conditioning formulae.
2.3.2-mean-variance-conditioning-cs1006..attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Apply E[Y] = E[E[Y|X]], then Var(Y) = E[Var(Y|X)] + Var(E[Y|X]).

steps.label: Apply the tower law for the mean
steps.attempt_cue: Average the conditional means with P(X).
steps.explanation: The law of total expectation recovers the unconditional mean from the conditional means.

steps.label: Form E[Var(Y|X)] and Var(E[Y|X])
steps.attempt_cue: Average the conditional variances, then variance the conditional means.
steps.explanation: Within-group variation is E[Var(Y|X)]. Between-group variation is Var(E[Y|X]) = E[m(X)²] − (E[m(X)])² with m(X) = E[Y|X].

steps.label: Add for Var(Y) and refuse stopping at E[Y|X]
steps.attempt_cue: Sum the two variance pieces and state why E[Y|X] alone is incomplete.
steps.explanation: Total variance is within plus between. Stopping after reporting E[Y|X] leaves both the unconditional mean (unless averaged) and the variance decomposition unfinished.

2.3.2-mean-variance-conditioning-cs1006..final_answer: E[Y] = 9.2; Var(Y) = 18.76, from E[Var(Y|X)] = 7 and Var(E[Y|X]) = 11.76.
2.3.2-mean-variance-conditioning-cs1006..common_pitfall: Reporting only E[Y|X] = 5 or 12 as if that finished the mean, or computing Var(Y) as E[Var(Y|X)] = 7 and omitting the between-group term Var(E[Y|X]) = 11.76.

2.4.1-mgf-cgf-cs1007.json.title: MGF and CGF for a Poisson claim count
2.4.1-mgf-cgf-cs1007.json.problem_statement: Annual claim count X ~ Poisson(λ = 2). Obtain the moment generating function M_X(t) and the cumulant generating function C_X(t). State why writing M_X(t) = 2 does not define the MGF.
2.4.1-mgf-cgf-cs1007.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Start from E[e^{tX}] for the Poisson pmf, then take the log for the CGF.

steps.label: Derive the Poisson MGF
steps.attempt_cue: Sum e^{tx} e^{-λ} λ^x / x! and recognise the series.
steps.explanation: For Poisson(λ), M_X(t) = exp(λ(e^t − 1)). With λ = 2 this is exp(2(e^t − 1)).

steps.label: Form the CGF
steps.attempt_cue: Take the natural log of the MGF.
steps.explanation: The CGF is C_X(t) = log M_X(t) = 2(e^t − 1).

steps.label: Refuse mean-as-MGF
steps.attempt_cue: State why M_X(t) = 2 is wrong even though E[X] = 2.
steps.explanation: The mean E[X] = 2 is M'(0) (or C'(0)), not the MGF itself. The MGF is a function of t, here exp(2(e^t − 1)), not the constant mean.

2.4.1-mgf-cgf-cs1007.json.final_answer: M_X(t) = exp(2(e^t − 1)); C_X(t) = 2(e^t − 1). The mean 2 is M'(0), not the MGF.
2.4.1-mgf-cgf-cs1007.json.common_pitfall: Writing M_X(t) = 2 or M_X(t) = e^{2t} because the mean is 2, instead of exp(2(e^t − 1)).

2.4.2-moment-via-gf-cs1007.json.title: Mean and variance from the Poisson CGF
2.4.2-moment-via-gf-cs1007.json.problem_statement: For X ~ Poisson(λ = 2), the cumulant generating function is C_X(t) = 2(e^t − 1). Obtain E[X] and Var(X) by differentiating the CGF at t = 0. Confirm that stopping at writing down C_X(t) without differentiation does not extract the moments.
2.4.2-moment-via-gf-cs1007.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Differentiate C once and twice, then evaluate at t = 0.

steps.label: Differentiate once for the mean
steps.attempt_cue: Compute C'(t) and evaluate at 0.
steps.explanation: C'(t) = 2e^t, so the first cumulant at the origin is the mean.

steps.label: Differentiate twice for the variance
steps.attempt_cue: Compute C''(t) and evaluate at 0.
steps.explanation: For this CGF, C''(t) = 2e^t as well, so the second cumulant equals the mean, as required for Poisson.

steps.label: Refuse definition-as-extraction
steps.attempt_cue: State why writing C_X(t) = 2(e^t − 1) alone does not give the moments.
steps.explanation: Having the generating function is not the same as extracting moments. Differentiation (or series expansion) at t = 0 is the extraction step.
steps.calculation: C_X(t) known ≠ moments extracted until C'(0), C''(0) evaluated

2.4.2-moment-via-gf-cs1007.json.final_answer: E[X] = C'(0) = 2; Var(X) = C''(0) = 2. Writing the CGF without differentiation does not extract the moments.
2.4.2-moment-via-gf-cs1007.json.common_pitfall: Treating the presence of C_X(t) = 2(e^t − 1) as already giving the moments, or evaluating C(0) = 0 and calling that the mean.

2.5.1-clt-cs1008.json.title: CLT probability for a mean pet-insurance severity
2.5.1-clt-cs1008.json.problem_statement: Pet-insurance claim severities are iid with mean μ = 180 and standard deviation σ = 60. A sample of n = 36 claims is drawn. Using the CLT, approximate P(X̄ < 170). Use Φ(1) ≈ 0.841.
2.5.1-clt-cs1008.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Form the sampling sd σ/√n first, then standardise 170 before reading Φ.

steps.label: Standard error of the sample mean
steps.attempt_cue: Compute σ/√n.
steps.explanation: Under the CLT for iid observations, X̄ is approximately Normal with mean μ and sd σ/√n.

steps.label: Standardise and evaluate the lower tail
steps.attempt_cue: Form z = (170 − 180)/10, then convert with Φ.
steps.explanation: The probability is the lower Normal tail at z = −1, equal to 1 − Φ(1).

steps.label: Refuse σ in place of σ/√n
steps.attempt_cue: State why using sd = 60 for X̄ is wrong.
steps.explanation: The CLT approximates the distribution of the sample mean, whose spread shrinks by √n. Using the population sd as if it were sd(X̄) ignores that reduction.

2.5.1-clt-cs1008.json.final_answer: X̄ ≈ Normal(180, 10); z = −1; P(X̄ < 170) ≈ 0.159. Casual Normal use without stating the IID CLT sampling sd is not the same skill.
2.5.1-clt-cs1008.json.common_pitfall: Using X̄ ≈ Normal(180, 60) and computing z = (170 − 180)/60 = −1/6, or reading Φ(1) ≈ 0.841 as the lower-tail probability itself.

2.5.2-simulated-sample-normal-cs1008.jso.title: Compare Exponential samples with a Normal overlay
2.5.2-simulated-sample-normal-cs1008.jso.problem_statement: Waiting times (days) follow Exponential with mean θ = 400 (so sd = 400 also). An analyst simulates samples of size n = 20 and overlays a Normal(400, 400²) density on the histogram of individual draws. Judge whether that Normal overlay is a good description of the individual-sample histogram, and state what changes if the object compared is instead the sampling distribution of X̄ at much larger n.
2.5.2-simulated-sample-normal-cs1008.jso.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Separate the shape of individual Exponential draws from the CLT behaviour of sample means before judging the overlay.

steps.label: Characterise the parent shape
steps.attempt_cue: Name the skewness feature of Exponential(400).
steps.explanation: An Exponential waiting-time law is right-skewed and supported on (0, ∞). Matching mean and sd to a Normal does not remove that skew for individual observations.
steps.calculation: Parent: right-skewed, support (0, ∞); Normal overlay is symmetric on (−∞, ∞)

steps.label: Judge the n = 20 individual-sample overlay
steps.attempt_cue: Decide whether Normal(400, 400²) describes the histogram of draws.
steps.explanation: At n = 20, simulated individual draws still show the Exponential skew and a hard floor at 0. A matched Normal puts mass on negative values and understates the right tail, so the overlay is a poor description of the sample histogram.
steps.calculation: Judgement: poor fit of Normal overlay to individual Exponential draws at n = 20
steps.result: Normal overlay fails for individual draws

steps.label: Contrast with the sample-mean story
steps.attempt_cue: State what improves when comparing sampling distributions of X̄ at large n.
steps.explanation: The CLT concerns the sample mean, not individual draws. Histograms of X̄ from many large-n replications become closer to Normal even when the parent is Exponential; that is a different comparison from overlaying Normal on raw waiting times.
steps.calculation: Individual draws: Normal poor; X̄ at large n: Normal approximation may improve
steps.result: Object of comparison matters (draws vs means)

2.5.2-simulated-sample-normal-cs1008.jso.final_answer: Normal(400, 400²) is a poor description of individual Exponential(400) draws at n = 20 (skew, support). Comparing sampling distributions of X̄ at large n is a different question where Normal approximation can improve.
2.5.2-simulated-sample-normal-cs1008.jso.common_pitfall: Treating a matched-mean-and-sd Normal overlay as automatically adequate for skewed individual draws, or confusing that histogram comparison with a CLT statement about X̄.

2.6.1-random-samples-cs1009.json.title: Classify a severity-truncated slice as not a random sample
2.6.1-random-samples-cs1009.json.problem_statement: An analyst keeps only the first 25 claims whose settled cost exceeds £10,000 from a national household book and treats that list as a random sample from all household claims in order to estimate portfolio mean severity. Decide whether this extract is a random sample from the stated population, and name the sampling defect.

given.value: all household claims in the national book

2.6.1-random-samples-cs1009.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Compare the severity-truncation mechanism with an iid (or otherwise stated) draw from all household claims before judging the sample label.

steps.label: State what a random sample requires
steps.attempt_cue: Name the warrant that links observations to the population distribution.
steps.explanation: A random sample is drawn so that observations follow the population distribution under a stated sampling model (for example iid draws). Estimators and intervals inherit that warrant.
steps.calculation: Require: stated sampling model linking extract to all-household-claim population
steps.result: Random sample = lawful draw under a sampling model

steps.label: Inspect the actual selection mechanism
steps.attempt_cue: Describe how the 25 claims were chosen.
steps.explanation: Keeping only claims above £10,000 truncates the severity distribution and over-represents large losses relative to the full household book. Order of arrival does not repair that truncation.
steps.calculation: Mechanism = severity truncation above £10,000 (selection on the outcome)
steps.result: Selection is truncated / outcome-dependent, not portfolio random

steps.label: Classify and refuse n-as-warrant
steps.attempt_cue: Decide yes/no on random sample, and say why n = 25 alone fails.
steps.explanation: Having twenty-five observations does not create a random sample. Without a lawful draw from all household claims, estimator procedures lack the sampling warrant.
steps.calculation: Classification: NOT a random sample from all household claims; defect = severity truncation / selection on Y
steps.result: Not a random sample; n alone is insufficient

2.6.1-random-samples-cs1009.json.final_answer: Not a random sample from all household claims: keeping only costs above £10,000 truncates severity. n = 25 does not by itself create a random sample.
2.6.1-random-samples-cs1009.json.common_pitfall: Treating any large enough extract as a random sample because n = 25 looks adequate, without checking whether the draw matches the stated all-claims population.

2.6.3-mean-var-sample-cs1009.json.title: Mean and variance of X̄ and mean of S²
2.6.3-mean-var-sample-cs1009.json.problem_statement: A population has mean μ = 12 and variance σ² = 36. A random sample of size n = 9 is drawn. Express E[X̄], Var(X̄), and E[S²] in terms of μ, σ², and n, and evaluate each numerically. Do not invoke Normal sampling laws or the t-statistic.
2.6.3-mean-var-sample-cs1009.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Use E[X̄] = μ, Var(X̄) = σ²/n, and E[S²] = σ² for the unbiased sample variance.

steps.label: Mean of the sample mean
steps.attempt_cue: State and evaluate E[X̄].
steps.explanation: For a random sample with finite mean, the sample mean is unbiased for μ.

steps.label: Variance of the sample mean
steps.attempt_cue: State and evaluate Var(X̄).
steps.explanation: Independence in the random sample gives Var(X̄) = σ²/n.

steps.label: Mean of S² and refuse Normal/t jump
steps.attempt_cue: State E[S²] and name what this LO does not yet require.
steps.explanation: For the usual unbiased sample variance, E[S²] = σ². This identity does not by itself give Normal laws for X̄ or the t-statistic; those need extra distributional assumptions treated in later LOs.
steps.result: E[S²] = 36; no Normal/t claim required here

2.6.3-mean-var-sample-cs1009.json.final_answer: E[X̄] = 12; Var(X̄) = 4; E[S²] = 36. These moment identities do not yet invoke Normal sampling laws or t.
2.6.3-mean-var-sample-cs1009.json.common_pitfall: Writing Var(X̄) = σ² = 36 instead of σ²/n = 4, or jumping to X̄ ~ Normal or a t pivot before this LO asks for it.

2.6.4-normal-sample-mean-var-cs1009.json.title: Normal laws for X̄ and for (n−1)S²/σ²
2.6.4-normal-sample-mean-var-cs1009.json.problem_statement: A random sample of size n = 16 is drawn from Normal(μ = 100, σ² = 25). State the exact sampling distribution of X̄ and of (n − 1)S²/σ². Explain why writing the t-statistic is a different object from these two laws.
2.6.4-normal-sample-mean-var-cs1009.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Write the Normal law for X̄ with variance σ²/n, then the chi-square law for the scaled sample variance, and keep t separate.

steps.label: Sampling distribution of X̄
steps.attempt_cue: Name the Normal parameters for X̄.
steps.explanation: For iid Normal observations, the sample mean is exactly Normal with mean μ and variance σ²/n.

steps.label: Sampling distribution of the scaled sample variance
steps.attempt_cue: State the chi-square law and its degrees of freedom.
steps.explanation: Independently of X̄, (n − 1)S²/σ² follows χ² with n − 1 degrees of freedom.

steps.label: Refuse treating this as the t-statistic
steps.attempt_cue: Name what extra ratio creates t.
steps.explanation: The t-statistic replaces σ with S in the studentised mean and uses the ratio of the Normal and chi-square pieces. Stating the separate Normal and χ² laws is not yet writing t = (X̄ − μ)/(S/√n).
steps.calculation: t uses (X̄ − μ)/(S/√n); that is not either law alone
steps.result: Normal and χ² laws ≠ the t-statistic

2.6.4-normal-sample-mean-var-cs1009.json.final_answer: X̄ ~ Normal(100, 1.5625); 15 S²/25 ~ χ²_15. The t-statistic is a further ratio that replaces σ by S, not either of these laws alone.
2.6.4-normal-sample-mean-var-cs1009.json.common_pitfall: Writing X̄ ~ Normal(100, 25) without dividing by n, or labelling (n − 1)S²/σ² ~ χ²_{n−1} as the t-statistic.

2.6.5-t-statistic-cs1009.json.title: Evaluate a one-sample t-statistic under Normal sampling
2.6.5-t-statistic-cs1009.json.problem_statement: A random sample of size n = 16 from a Normal population yields X̄ = 105 and sample standard deviation S = 8. Under H₀: μ = 100, compute the t-statistic and state its null degrees of freedom. Explain why replacing S by the unknown σ in a z formula is not available here.
2.6.5-t-statistic-cs1009.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Form t = (X̄ − μ₀)/(S/√n) and name df = n − 1.

steps.label: Form the standard error using S
steps.attempt_cue: Compute S/√n.
steps.explanation: With σ unknown, the studentised mean uses the sample sd in the denominator.

steps.label: Evaluate t and degrees of freedom
steps.attempt_cue: Compute (X̄ − μ₀)/SE and df.
steps.explanation: Under Normal sampling and H₀, t follows Student-t with n − 1 degrees of freedom.

steps.label: Refuse z-with-S and F swallow
steps.attempt_cue: State why a z pivot with S is not the t law, and why F is a different job.
steps.explanation: Using S inside a Normal z formula pretends σ is known. The t law accounts for estimating σ. An F comparison of two sample variances is a different sampling problem from this one-sample mean pivot.
steps.calculation: z-with-S ≠ t_{15}; F is for variance ratios, not this mean pivot
steps.result: Use t_{15}, not z-with-S or F

2.6.5-t-statistic-cs1009.json.final_answer: t = 2.5 on 15 degrees of freedom. With σ unknown, the correct pivot is t, not a z that plugs in S, and not an F variance-ratio statistic.
2.6.5-t-statistic-cs1009.json.common_pitfall: Computing z = (105 − 100)/(8/4) = 2.5 and treating it as standard Normal because the arithmetic matches t, or reaching for an F statistic when the question is about a single mean.

2.6.6-f-distribution-cs1009.json.title: Variance-ratio F from two independent Normal samples
2.6.6-f-distribution-cs1009.json.problem_statement: Two independent random samples are drawn from Normal populations with equal variances. Sample 1 has n₁ = 10 and S₁² = 20; sample 2 has n₂ = 8 and S₂² = 10. Form the variance-ratio statistic F = S₁² / S₂², state its null distribution (degrees of freedom), and explain why a one-sample t-statistic is the wrong tool for this comparison.

given.note: second Normal sample, independent of the first

2.6.6-f-distribution-cs1009.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Form the ratio of sample variances and attach F(df₁, df₂) with df = n − 1 for each sample.

steps.label: Form the variance ratio
steps.attempt_cue: Compute F = S₁² / S₂².
steps.explanation: For independent Normal samples, the ratio of unbiased sample variances is the natural comparison of scale under equal-variance nulls.

steps.label: State the null F distribution
steps.attempt_cue: Name degrees of freedom for numerator and denominator.
steps.explanation: Under σ₁² = σ₂², F ~ F(n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1) = F(9, 7).

steps.label: Refuse using t for that job
steps.attempt_cue: State why a t pivot for a mean is the wrong tool here.
steps.explanation: The t-statistic studentises a mean using one sample's S. Comparing two variances uses the F ratio of sample variances. Substituting a t critical value or a one-sample mean pivot does not answer the variance-ratio question.
steps.calculation: t studentises a mean; F compares two sample variances

2.6.6-f-distribution-cs1009.json.final_answer: F = 2 ~ F(9, 7) under equal variances. A t-statistic for a mean is the wrong tool for a two-sample variance comparison.
2.6.6-f-distribution-cs1009.json.common_pitfall: Using t with pooled sd to compare variances, or assigning F degrees of freedom as n₁ and n₂ instead of n₁ − 1 and n₂ − 1.
